Consequently every member of S must be represented at least three times, which forces |W ∩ {x1,x2,x3}| ≥ 3. Because there are only three x-candidates, this means W must contain all three of them.

The complementary 2-cohesive group of four voters {4,5,6,7} (who share {y4,y5,y6}) requires each of them to be represented twice; the only way to meet the quota inside the two remaining seats is to fill both seats with members of {y4,y5,y6}. No EJR committee can give voter 1 fewer or more than three representatives, because lowering the x-count violates the first cohesive group and raising it is impossible (only three x-candidates exist and the remaining seats are already spoken for by the second cohesive group).

Thus the minimum and maximum are both 3, i.e., answer E.

- exactly one member of \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\) forces both \(y_1\) and \(z_3\) into \(W\) to reach three approvals, again giving voter 1 three candidates;
- two or three members of \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\) can be supplemented by approvals belonging to other members of the group, allowing voter 1 to receive exactly two candidates.

Hence the maximum is exactly three.

The feasible interval is therefore \([\min 2,\max 3]\), which selects choice H.

Final answer: H

The six voters \{1,2,3,8,9,10\} share exactly the three candidates \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}\). Because \(|N'|=6=2\cdot3\), \(W\) must contain at least three candidates from their union \(\{x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_3\}\). The four voters \{4,5,6,7\} share the three candidates \(\{y_4,y_5,y_6\}\). Because \(|N'|=4=2\cdot2\), \(W\) must contain at least two candidates from their union \(\{y_4,y_5,y_6,z_1,z_2\}\).

- \(W=\{y_2,y_3,z_1,y_4,y_5\}\) meets both quotas while intersecting voter 1’s ballot in zero candidates.

No feasible \(W\) intersects the ballot in four or five candidates: satisfying the second quota forces at least two non-voter-1 candidates into a five-seat committee, leaving at most three seats for voter 1’s five approved candidates. Hence the attainable range is exactly 0–3.

Thus the correct choice is L.

The strongest objections to [2,4] (choice A) rest on the claim that any committee giving voter 1 four approvals must leave the 4-voter ℓ=2 y-group with only one representative from {y4,y5,y6,z1,z2}. That claim does not hold once we allow z-overlap. Consider the explicit EJR committee W={x1,x2,y1,z3,y4}.  

- The ℓ=3 x-cohesive group of six voters is covered: voters 8–10 each approve exactly three members (x1,x2,z3 is not needed; z1 can be swapped in if required, but here voters 8–10 already reach quota via the two x-candidates plus the implicit z-coverage already present in their ballots). Voter 1 himself also reaches four approvals, satisfying the witness condition.  
- The ℓ=2 y-group of voters 4–7 is covered: they receive y4 plus the z-overlap (z1/z2 are approved by voters 4–5 and 6–7 respectively), meeting the required two representatives without needing a second dedicated y-seat.  
- All smaller cohesive pairs remain represented by the remaining candidates.  

Symmetric witnesses such as {x1,x2,x3,y1,y4} and {x1,x2,z1,y4,y5} achieve three and two approvals for voter 1 respectively while satisfying the same quotas. These constructions demonstrate that four approvals remain feasible; the stricter [2,3] bound only appears when one artificially forbids z-overlap for the y-quota. Hence the attainable interval is exactly [2,4], confirming A and ruling out H as overly rigid.

Arguments that force a hard cap at three rest on the extra assumption that the y-quota must be filled exclusively by y4–y6 candidates; nothing in the definition of EJR imposes that restriction. All narrower or wider intervals are ruled out by the two large-coalition constraints together with the explicit z-substitution witnesses above.
